name: Middle High German

ancestors.notes: Descent from Old High German; Paul, Mittelhochdeutsche Grammatik

notes: Middle High German (c. 1050-1500), ancestor of the modern High German and Hunsrik varieties. The grapheme table targets the normalised orthography (Lachmann) with circumflex length, iu=/yː/, æ/œ umlaut vowels, but the shipped wikipron gold (gmh_latn_broad, n=1516) instead follows English Wiktionary's own article-title spelling convention (0 circumflex vowels and 0 ë tokens across the gold's 1724 source words, against 115 words carrying æ/œ and 130 carrying ä/ö/ü — see `gmh-x-wikt.json` and docs/gold_defects.md). That is a distinct, sourced orthography for the same language, not a reason to drop the circumflex/ë entries here, which are correct for edited normalised MHG text; the wikipron gold should be scored against `gmh-x-wikt`, which inherits this spec's phonology whole via `graphemes_base`. Unstressed inflectional ⟨e⟩ (Nebensilbenvokal) reduces to schwa; ⟨s⟩ is the apical fricative [s̠] distinct from dorsal ⟨z⟩; ⟨tz⟩/⟨zz⟩ spell the geminate affricate/fricative outcomes of the High German Consonant Shift. A bare, non-doubled ⟨z⟩ is genuinely ambiguous between the affricate and fricative reflex in this orthography (the historical z1/z2 problem some editions resolve with a diacritic ȝ that this gold does not use); it is left as the affricate default and not fitted to the gold. Measured per-change against the wikipron gold (n=1516, baseline PER 0.2938): the unstressed-e schwa reduction alone moves PER to 0.1667 (the dominant contributor); the apical ⟨s⟩ fix alone moves it to 0.2478; the ⟨tz⟩/⟨zz⟩ geminate split alone (tie bar aside) moves it to 0.2752; combined, PER is 0.1022. The [t͡s] tie bar on the bare ⟨z⟩ affricate is written for linguistic correctness only and contributes nothing to PER — the benchmark normalizer strips tie bars before comparison.

stress.notes: Middle High German inherits the Germanic root-initial stress rule: primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root, before any inflectional or (most) derivational affixes; unstressed prefixes (ge-, be-, ent- etc.) and borrowed words are not modeled here. Source: Paul, Mittelhochdeutsche Grammatik (rev. Klein, Solms & Wegera, 2007), stress chapter.
